paragraphs: This list is for self-questioning only and does not constitute recruitment criteria, a capability score, or a conclusion evaluating food service operations and management. This page is written according to the US O*NET-SOC 11-9051.00 'Food Service Managers' (the fixed index gives this asset the Chinese name whose English rendering is 'Food service managers'; the main objects are planning, directing or coordinating the daily activities of an establishment or department that provides food and beverages).

Paper exercise | use the complete fictional one-day task below: 100 at lunch and 130 at dinner (both including banquets); two shifts each with 2 prep and 2 service staff, eight people at 4 hours each; existing stock 20, planned purchase 210, of which 10 are damaged on acceptance. Within 90 minutes produce the scheduling, inventory purchasing, cost and anomaly handover sheets and compare them against the reference answer; a purchase exceeding authorisation by 20 yuan, a shortfall of 10 on the pass and a B2 allergy menu conflict must be reported to M1, without touching real meals or personal data.

Fit signals | O*NET points of focus: teamwork extremely important (97%), continuous contact with others (94%), face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams every day (93%), working indoors in an environmentally controlled environment every day (91%), dealing with external customers or the public extremely important (84%), telephone conversations every day (80%), making decisions every day (70%), leading or coordinating others extremely important (66%), very high responsibility for the work results of others (65%), standing continually or almost continually (65%). If you are willing to organise schedules and stock around fluctuating customer flow and can face dense interpersonal contact and on-site decisions and complaint pressure, the daily requirements of this occupation are closer to your way of working.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows: the impact of decisions on colleagues and company results very important (66%), dealing with unpleasant or angry or discourteous people once a week or more (56%), very high responsibility for the health and safety of other workers (51%), physically close to others (49%), wearing protective or safety equipment every day (49%), time pressure once a week or more (45%), conflict situations once a week or more (45%), a typical working week of more than 40 hours (41%). Operational errors can directly affect food safety, alcohol and fire safety compliance and the safety of employees and customers, and carry budget and employment responsibility. If you find it hard to bear continuous on-site decisions, evening and weekend and holiday shifts, and the pressure of customer and employee conflict, treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Taking on the judgement | real fit comes from being able to do three things in the same week: organise operations (schedule shifts and stock around customer flow and banquet orders, monitor output and hygiene, maintain service standards), keep costs and personnel under control (budget and payroll and menu cost accounting and pricing, recruitment and training and assessment, handover and record keeping), and take on reviewable compliance and escalation responsibility (food preparation and hygiene, alcohol and age verification, fire safety and equipment hazards, handling and reporting complaints and labour disputes). It is suggested to test this through one verifiable experience (working alongside a shift at a food service outlet or acting as duty assistant, completing a simulated scheduling and cost accounting and compliance inspection exercise, or attending food safety and alcohol and service management training and passing a practical assessment), rather than relying only on the conclusion of an interest questionnaire.

Safety work sample | the complete inputs and reference answer are in the one-day fictional task in the entry module. Submit within 90 minutes the schedule of 32 labour hours, the inventory and 230 portion requirement check, the purchase budget, the planned balance and the anomaly handover; simulated acceptance records must not be treated as authorised purchasing, nor unconfirmed meals written up as served.

Scope and boundaries | plan, direct or coordinate the activities of an establishment or department that provides food and beverages, managing scheduling, purchasing and acceptance and inventory, service and food preparation quality, budget and payroll, personnel training and complaints. O*NET also lists cooking, clearing tables and food and beverage service when necessary, and some menu design tasks; these overlap with adjacent positions. The occupational classification itself does not confer licensing, professional sign-off or enforcement authority, and specific duties and decision authority must be verified against local regulations and the employer's appointment.

entries: Operational planning and customer flow forecasting | scheduling and job duties | forecast labour for each period by customer flow and banquet orders, prepare schedules and assign front-of-house and back-of-house job duties.

Purchasing and inventory control | food and beverage and equipment | order and accept food, beverages and equipment per the menu and forecast consumption, maintain inventory records and control loss and waste.

Quality and compliance monitoring | preparation and hygiene and fire safety | monitor food preparation methods, portion sizes and hygiene and alcohol regulations and fire safety compliance, handling deviations with records.

Finance and cost accounting | budget and payroll and pricing | monitor budget and payroll and turnover, cost the menu and set prices, and review whether expenditure is within authorisation and budget.

Personnel and team management | recruitment and training and assessment | assess labour needs and recruit and train and schedule, handle employee issues and complete performance assessments and handovers.

Customers and complaints and records | complaints and reservations and record keeping | receive and handle customer complaints and reservations, record sales and compliance and operational records and complete shift and handover duties.

paragraphs:
Work context | the O*NET 11-9051.00 work context shows (the percentages below are the distribution of respondent answers, not individual working hours or accident rates): the work is dominated by teamwork and on-site decisions and contact with external customers, mostly in a controlled indoor environment.
Environmental conditions | working indoors in an environmentally controlled environment every day (91%), with a tight work pace and possible exposure to high heat and noise.
Protective equipment | wearing routine protective or safety equipment every day (49%).

Standing and moving about | standing continually or almost continually (65%), walking or running continually or almost continually (44%).
Contact and collaboration | continuous contact with others (94%), face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams every day (93%), teamwork extremely important (97%), leading or coordinating others extremely important (66%), physically close to others (49%).

External contact and communication | dealing with external customers or the public extremely important (84%), telephone conversations every day (80%), using email every day (59%).
Decisions and freedom | making decisions every day (70%), decision freedom considerable (47%), some freedom to determine tasks and priorities (42%), time pressure at least once a week but not every day (45%).

Precision and repetition | precision or accuracy extremely important (40%), repeating the same task important (36%), repetitive motion less than half the time (35%).

Responsibility and consequences | very high responsibility for the work results of others (65%), the impact of decisions on colleagues and company results very important (66%), very high responsibility for the health and safety of other workers (51%), dealing with unpleasant or angry or discourteous people (56%) and conflict situations (45%) at least once a week but not every day, and a typical working week of more than 40 hours (41%).

Environment and pace | the workplace is restaurants and chain outlets, hotel food and beverage departments, school and institutional canteens, and banquet and catering venues. It is mostly indoors in a controlled environment (91% every day), but kitchens and banquet venues involve high heat, noise and wet and slippery differences. The work pace is determined by meal periods, banquet orders and weekend and holiday customer flow, with evening and weekend and holiday shifts common and possible call-backs (a typical working week of more than 40 hours accounts for 41%). The physical load is concentrated in continuous standing (65%) and walking (44%) and frequent interpersonal contact, while also carrying the pressure of continuous decisions and anomaly handling on budget, personnel and compliance.

Tools and materials | equipment: point-of-sale (POS) systems, scheduling and reservation systems, inventory and purchasing systems, finance and payroll management systems, office and spreadsheet software, kitchen and banquet equipment and holding and refrigeration equipment, and cleaning and sanitising equipment. Materials: food and beverages and drinks and disposables, menus and recipes and cost cards, hygiene and alcohol and fire safety compliance documents and checklists, and protective equipment. Documents: sales and inventory and payroll and budget records, complaint and work order records, training and assessment records, and licensing and compliance documents. All menu and pricing and compliance judgements are subject to the enterprise rules valid for that shift and to local regulations.

Forecast customer flow and schedule staff → order and accept and hold inventory → monitor preparation and hygiene and compliance → account for costs and price → handle complaints and personnel issues → record and hand over and report

Quality standards | operations should organise scheduling and stock around customer flow and banquet orders: positions fully staffed in each period, food and beverage accepted to standard, output portions and hygiene meeting standards, budget and payroll and turnover within the authorised range, and complaints and anomalies recorded and closed out. Anything inconsistent with food preparation and hygiene, alcohol regulations, fire safety compliance or the scope of authorisation must first be discussed with the relevant responsible person or licensed personnel with a record left, and compliance requirements must not be relaxed on your own or acceptance and authorisation bypassed.

Adjacent responsibilities | this occupation manages a food and beverage establishment or department; first-line supervisors focus on on-site execution, head chefs focus on dishes and the kitchen, accommodation managers focus on lodging, and general operations managers have a broader scope. Actual organisations may combine roles or cross-assign tasks, and O*NET explicitly lists menu design, cooking, service and licensing and tax and payroll document tasks for this occupation; these cannot all be excluded or sign-off authority assigned by job title alone. Specific statutory qualifications and matters beyond authority are verified separately.

Boundary review suggestion | where food safety, alcohol sales or age verification, fire equipment hazards, over-budget authorisation or escalation of employee complaints are found, handle and record them per local rules and enterprise processes. Licensing and tax and payroll documents may be part of the manager's tasks; only matters beyond position authority or involving statutory qualifications should be referred to the appropriate responsible person or specialist position, and the occupational classification cannot be used to infer that none of these may be handled.
Forecast and schedule → order and accept → monitor and comply → account and price → handle complaints and personnel → record and hand over and report

Difference from first-line-supervisors-of-food-preparation-and-serving-workers: the latter focuses on on-site execution supervision and schedule delivery for a single shift and specific positions; this occupation carries overall responsibility for budget, purchasing, menu pricing, personnel recruitment and compliance, with a broader scope of authority and responsibility.

Difference from head chefs and executive chefs | the latter focus on cooking technique, menus and kitchen output; this occupation focuses on the operations, cost and personnel management of the establishment or department. O*NET also lists cooking and service and some menu design tasks for this occupation, and actual divisions of work may overlap.

Adjacent position check | compare the objects and work focus of on-site supervision, kitchen technique, accommodation operations and institutional coordination; duties may overlap and adjacent titles cannot define absolute authority boundaries. Specific recruitment, employer appointment and local rules are verified separately.

Difference from accommodation and general operations managers | accommodation managers focus on lodging facilities and guest services, and general operations managers focus on the organisation's overall goals and resources; this occupation focuses on the establishment or department that provides food and beverages. The organisational level depends on the employer's appointment and cannot be inferred from the occupational title.

Before choosing this occupation, compare: the real tasks (the proportion of scheduling and purchasing and cost and personnel and compliance), qualification and training paths (relevant work experience, food safety and alcohol and fire safety and service management training), shifts and pressure (evening and weekend and holiday shifts, customer flow fluctuation and complaint and employment pressure), and growth paths (moving to first-line supervisor, head chef, accommodation manager, general and operations manager, or starting a food business). Different settings (chain outlets, independent restaurants, hotel food and beverage, institutional canteens and banquet services) vary considerably and should be verified against actual recruitment and on-site experience.

Responsibility boundaries cannot be inferred from the similarity of job titles: although all are food service and management positions, on-site execution supervision, dish technique, accommodation operations, overall organisational strategy and food and beverage department operations differ in authority and output. Cross-position work requires relearning processes and authorisation and compliance requirements, and the original position's judgement and sign-off authority cannot be carried over; matters involving food safety incidents, labour disputes, alcohol licensing and fire safety acceptance must be borne by the corresponding responsible parties.

AI task exposure | digital tools may assist with scheduling and customer flow forecasting, inventory and purchasing reminders, sales and cost analysis, complaint and work order tracking, draft training materials and generating compliance checklists. But on-site supervision of food preparation and hygiene and service, personnel management and complaint handling, and judgements on alcohol regulations and fire safety compliance remain with managers and responsible persons holding the corresponding duties and authorisation; task exposure does not equal job replacement.

Occupational definition | plan, direct or coordinate the activities of an establishment or department that provides food and beverages, managing scheduling, purchasing and acceptance and inventory, service and food preparation quality, budget and payroll, personnel training and complaints. O*NET also lists cooking, clearing tables and food and beverage service when necessary, and some menu design tasks; these overlap with adjacent positions. The occupational classification itself does not confer licensing, professional sign-off or enforcement authority, and specific duties and decision authority must be verified against local regulations and the employer's appointment.

Data and system thresholds | before adoption, verify: whether sales and inventory and payroll data can be traced back to the original shift and vouchers; the permissions and update and retention mechanisms for customer and employee information; whether scheduling and cost and loss definitions are consistent; whether systems can degrade to manual forms and retain records during network or terminal failure; and the data consistency and permission requirements for interfaces with supplier and payment and tax systems.

Human control points and manual review | scheduling and labour decisions, purchasing and acceptance, menu pricing and cost judgements, food preparation and hygiene supervision, complaint and labour dispute handling, and alcohol and fire safety compliance checks must be completed by managers or responsible persons holding the corresponding duties and authorisation; any forecast, reminder, report or checklist generated by a tool must be manually checked with a trace left before use.

Residual responsibility | matters that must not be released automatically: whether food preparation and hygiene and alcohol and fire safety compliance are met, whether expenditure is within authorisation and budget, handling of employment and labour disputes, the truthfulness of licensing and compliance declarations, and decisions involving closure or service interruption. No tool output equals a pass conclusion or an authorisation decision.

Failure risk | unreviewed tool outputs may cause inaccurate scheduling and costs, uncontrolled purchasing and inventory, pricing and budget deviation, missed compliance checks, or treating unconfirmed employment and handling plans as established, creating food safety and compliance and financial and labour dispute risk. Before deployment, make clear who reviews and against what original vouchers.

Employment evidence boundaries | the employment and wage data of this occupation must be distinguished by definition: the US figures from O*NET and the BLS are estimates under a specific statistical definition and cannot be extrapolated directly to mainland China or other regions; China uses industry category average wages as a background proxy, which does not constitute an occupational wage conclusion. Anything generated should be traceable back to the original inputs and sources, and fluent wording must not be treated as correct evidence.

Practical response | first put digital tools into low-risk steps that can be rolled back and audited (scheduling and inventory reminders, sales and cost reports, complaint work order tracking, draft training materials), subject to confirmation by managers and responsible persons holding the corresponding duties and authorisation and to actual operations; decide whether to expand the scope of use based on errors and complaints and compliance incidents, and always keep manual confirmation for cost and employment and compliance judgements.

Cross-market definition boundaries | mainland China and the United States have different industry and occupational classification systems: mainland China publishes the average wage of employed persons in urban units by national economic industry category, without listing this occupation separately; the United States gives estimates by SOC occupation and industry. The two cannot be spliced or converted, and industry averages cannot replace occupational wages.

Insufficient evidence: the National Bureau of Statistics publications reviewed do not list public occupational wage statistics precisely corresponding to 'food service managers'; industry averages, recruitment quotes or third-party estimates are not used as substitutes.

Mainland China wage evidence review points | this page provides only statistical definitions, industry background proxies and a register of visible gaps, and does not provide an estimated wage for this occupation. Before using any figure, first confirm whether its statistical definition (industry category / occupation), statistical period, unit of measurement and covered population are comparable with this occupation.

US wage definition | May 2025 OEWS includes basic wages, production bonuses, commissions and tips; it excludes overtime, shift differentials, non-production bonuses and employer benefits, and does not cover the self-employed. National percentiles are not experience grades, nor are they an individual's contract income.

China coverage | NBS covers employed persons in legal entities with 5 or more persons in urban areas; sole proprietors and the self-employed are outside the scope; chain, franchise or outsourced status itself does not determine coverage and the specific unit must be verified. The accommodation and food service industry average is not this occupation's statistic and does not cover all settings such as hospitals.

Insufficient evidence: no occupational wage median for food service managers that can be verified by occupation was obtained for mainland China; industry category averages are not used as substitutes.

Mainland China wage evidence — statistical period | industry average wages are an annual definition (the figures below are for 2025, published in 2026), which differs from the US May 2025 point-in-time wage on this page, and the two periods cannot be mixed.

Cross-market definition boundaries | mainland China industry average wages and US occupational wages differ in statistical object, period and definition; this page presents them separately with their limitations noted, does not perform currency conversion, and does not treat industry averages as occupational wages.

Unit of measurement | Chinese industry annual average wages are pre-tax yuan / year, including bonuses and the personal income tax, personal social insurance and housing provident fund withheld by the employer. US OEWS is in US dollars / hour or US dollars / year, including production bonuses, commissions and tips and excluding overtime, non-production bonuses and employer benefits; it does not cover the self-employed. The two cannot be compared directly.

Insufficient evidence: no food service manager wage data verifiable by region or employment form was obtained for mainland China; individual quotes or second-hand accounts are not used as substitutes.

Covered population | the NBS survey covers employed persons in urban legal entities with 5 or more persons and excludes sole proprietors and the self-employed; the accommodation and food service industry is not the occupational statistic for food service managers and does not cover all settings of this occupation such as hospitals.

US wage evidence — market definition | BLS OEWS is a sample survey estimate representing wages reported by employers and excludes the self-employed (owner-operators of restaurants are not counted). The median represents the midpoint of the distribution and is not a starting wage, nor does it represent any single region or employer.

US wage evidence — statistical period | the wage is May 2025 OEWS; employment, growth and openings are from the 2025—2035 employment projections. The two types of data have different reference points and must not be mixed into a conclusion for the same point in time.

US wage evidence — unit of measurement | published in 'US dollars / hour' and 'US dollars / year'; the annual average wage is converted on a full-year full-time basis, and converting between hourly and annual values does not equal personal actual income, which is also affected by hours, bonuses and allowances and business conditions.

Covered population | OEWS is a wage employee estimate and does not include the self-employed. The employment projections are a different programme that includes the self-employed; the 2025 projection base period for this occupation is 344,300 people with the self-employed accounting for 30.6%, while OEWS May2025 employment is 238,430 people; the whole difference between the two values is not attributed to self-employment, nor are they treated as the same programme.

US wage evidence — occupational scope | the figures on this page correspond to SOC 11-9051 (Food Service Managers); they exclude first-line supervisors of food preparation and serving workers (35-1012), head chefs and executive chefs (35-1011), accommodation managers (11-9081), general and operations managers (11-1021), food counter attendants (fast food and counter service) (35-3023), food preparation workers (35-2021), waiters and waitresses (35-3031) and bartenders (35-3011). Wages across occupations must not be mixed.

Sampling and scope | May2025 OEWS employment is 238,430 people, with a relative standard error of employment of 1.7%; the projection base period is 344,300 people and includes the self-employed. The programme populations differ and the difference cannot be directly subtracted to explain the cause. Four high-annual-median industry examples have been obtained from the current official interface, for industry comparison rather than as a main employer or individual opportunity.

paragraphs: Conclusion | the core difference between this occupation and adjacent occupations is 'scope of authority and outputs': this occupation plans, directs or coordinates the daily operations of a food service department and carries responsibility for budget, purchasing, menu cost and pricing, and personnel recruitment and training and compliance; first-line supervisors focus on on-site execution supervision for a single shift and specific positions; head chefs and executive chefs are responsible for menu and dish design and kitchen output; accommodation managers are responsible for lodging facility operations and guest experience; general and operations managers are responsible for the organisation's overall operations and strategy; food counter attendants (fast food and counter service) and food preparation workers and waiters and waitresses carry out frontline work. Authority and outputs differ, and judgement and sign-off authority cannot be carried across positions.

Evidence note | the comparison objects in the table below come from the O*NET occupational classification and current public occupational materials, and are used to help distinguish the work content of adjacent occupations and choose a fit; they do not constitute qualification, recruitment or compensation conclusions. The wages and employment of each occupation must be verified separately under their own SOC definitions, and this table does not compare figures or treat one occupation's wage as a proxy for another's.

Preface | the following comparison is laid out in four columns: 'occupational direction — core work and outputs — key differences — what it is a better choice for'. Food service positions are often linked by process, but linkage does not equal substitutability; when choosing across directions, the setting, scope of authority and compliance requirements must be relearned.

Centred on the daily operations management of a food service department: scheduling shifts and stock around customer flow and banquet orders, monitoring output and hygiene and alcohol and fire safety compliance, accounting for budget and payroll and menu cost and pricing, recruitment and training and assessment, and handling customer complaints and employee issues with records.

Better suited to people willing to organise operations amid fluctuating customer flow and complaint pressure, who can take on budget and employment and compliance responsibility, and who are used to managing the floor with records and reviews.

Output is sustainable food service operations: scheduling and stock plans, compliance monitoring and rectification records, cost and pricing and budget records, personnel and training and assessment records, and complaint and anomaly handling and handover records.
This occupation: food service managers

Centred on on-site position execution supervision for a single shift: organise meal service and service pace per the schedule, supervise hygiene and operating standards, handle shift anomalies and hand over upward.
Better suited to people willing to lead a single shift on the floor and watch execution; those who prefer carrying overall responsibility for budget and personnel and compliance fit this occupation.
Output is the shift's execution results: position staffing and meal service and service records, shift inspection and rectification records, and anomaly reporting and handover records.
First-Line Supervisors of Food Preparation and Serving Workers
Centred on menus and dish design and kitchen output: developing and testing and standardising recipes, organising kitchen output and output standards, and controlling kitchen costs and hygiene.
Better suited to people who prefer dish technique and kitchen output standards; those who prefer overall responsibility for operations and finance and personnel management fit this occupation.
Output is dishes and kitchen output: standard recipes and output, dish cost and technique records, and kitchen hygiene and output inspection records.
Chefs and Head Cooks

Centred on lodging facility operations and guest experience: room and front desk and reservation and lodging service arrangements, lodging cost and personnel management, and guest experience and complaint handling.
Better suited to people who prefer a lodging setting and the guest's end-to-end experience; those who prefer food service department operations and cost and compliance fit this occupation.
Output is lodging operations and guest experience: room and front desk service arrangements, lodging cost and personnel records, and guest complaint and experience improvement records.
Lodging Managers

Centred on the organisation's overall operations and strategy: coordinating departmental goals and resources, setting business strategy and assessment, and being responsible for overall profit and loss and compliance.

Better suited to people who take on organisation-level goals and cross-departmental coordination; this occupation usually focuses on the operations and compliance responsibility of a food service department.

Output is the organisation's overall business results: departmental goals and resource arrangements, business strategy and assessment documents, and overall profit and loss and compliance conclusions.
General and Operations Managers
Centred on ordering and meal assembly and cashiering and counter service: taking orders and assembling meals, cashiering and change and cleaning, customer service and handover.
Better suited to people who prefer fast-paced frontline execution; those who prefer organising schedules and accounting for costs and compliance management fit this occupation.
Output is frontline service and settlement: order and meal and cashier records, shift cleaning and stocking records, and customer service and anomaly handover.
Fast Food and Counter Workers

Transition | this page sets adjacent positions side by side by 'scope of authority and outputs', to help you judge which kind of food service and management setting you want to invest in long term. Whichever direction you choose, what really determines whether you can take up the work is your understanding of processes and compliance and employment requirements, your ability to organise the floor and keep records under customer flow and complaint pressure, and passing practical work and assessment accepted by the employer or supervisor; an interest questionnaire is only for raising questions.

What personality is it suited to? This occupation values responsibility, organisation and communication and compliance awareness more than any personality type; the O*NET interest code is ECR (Enterprising—Conventional—Realistic) and can serve as a starting point for exploration.

Introverts can also explore it, but suitability cannot be judged by introversion and extroversion alone; this occupation involves continuous contact with others 94% and face-to-face contact every day 93%, so the communication and conflict requirements should be experienced in practice.

What should you prepare before entering? First understand the real pace (evening and weekend and holiday shifts, customer flow fluctuation and complaint and employment pressure, a working week often over 40 hours) and prepare basic knowledge of food service and cost and food safety and alcohol and fire safety compliance; you can start as a duty supervisor or operations assistant.

Physical tasks | 65% of respondents answered continuous standing and 44% continuous walking, which are respondent distributions, not each person's share of working hours. The O*NET figures of standing 65% and walking 44% are respondent context answers; safety measures are verified against the actual site and personal long-term health is not predicted from shifts.

Career cycle and transition directions? You can grow from duty supervisor to outlet manager and regional management, or move to head chef and executive chef, lodging manager, general and operations manager and food service entrepreneurship; changing direction requires relearning processes and authorisation and compliance requirements.

Article 44 of China's Food Safety Law requires food production and operation enterprises to train employees, and Article 45 requires those in contact with directly edible food to undergo an annual examination and obtain a health certificate before taking up the post; the operating licence belongs to the operator, and training or a health certificate does not automatically confer pricing, employment or clinical judgement authority.

values: A completely fictional one-day outlet; 100 at lunch (80 standard plus 20 of B1 for banquets) and 130 at dinner (100 standard plus 30 of B2 for banquets); banquets are already counted in the period totals and are not added again. Uniform price 30 yuan per portion and food cost 12 yuan; existing acceptable stock 20 portions, planned purchase 210 portions; the exercise purchase authorisation limit is 2500 yuan and any excess must be reported to the responsible person M1.

Two shifts, 11:00–15:00 and 17:00–21:00, each requiring 2 prep and 2 service staff. C1–C4 can prep and P1–P4 can serve, each person may take one shift of at most 4 hours that day, and the simulated hourly wage is 25 yuan. Fixed simulated other costs 400 yuan; taxes, depreciation and other unlisted costs are not counted.

Delivery record: of the 210 portions, 10 have damaged packaging and are awaiting isolation, and 200 meet the acceptance standard set in the task; the 10 damaged portions are not counted as usable stock. B2 adds a peanut allergy notice, but the current simulated menu contains peanuts and no safe alternative menu or reply from the responsible person has been provided.

Task outputs may be on paper or in a spreadsheet: shift / personnel / position / hours; quantity / stock / purchase / acceptance / shortfall; revenue and cost calculation; anomalies / suspension status / report to M1 / matters awaiting reply. Time limit 90 minutes. All values and rules are exercise inputs, not real outlet standards or wage levels.
Complete the staffing arrangements for both shifts, the portion and stock purchase calculation, and the budget and planned balance calculation, distinguishing planned from executed status.

For the purchase over authorisation, the damaged acceptance, the shortfall and the allergy menu conflict, write separately the suspension or isolation, the basis for checking and the report to M1 awaiting reply; you must not release them yourself or invent approval.

Deliver a one-page shift summary and four tables; mark the simulated data, what you completed and what has not been reviewed. Do not use real employee, customer or enterprise information, and do not carry out actual purchasing or catering.

One scheduling reference: lunch C1/C2 prep and P1/P2 service; dinner C3/C4 prep and P3/P4 service. Each shift is 4 people × 4 hours = 16 labour hours, 32 labour hours for the day, labour 32 × 25 = 800 yuan; other arrangements that meet the qualifications set in the task and the 4-hour limit per person are also acceptable.

Requirement 100+130=230 portions; 20 in stock, 210 planned to be purchased, and the purchase 210 × 12 = 2520 yuan exceeds the 2500 authorisation by 20 yuan, so report to M1 first and do not execute the purchase without authorisation. The delivery situation is the acceptance record set in the task and does not mean the purchase is approved; the acceptable 200 + the original 20 = 220, still 10 short. The 10 damaged portions are isolated, and replenishment and whether to adjust catering must be confirmed by M1.

Planned revenue 230 × 30 = 6900, food 230 × 12 = 2760, labour 800, fixed 400, planned balance 6900 − 2760 − 800 − 400 = 2940 yuan; this is not a complete net profit or money received, and unlisted taxes and depreciation must not be treated as a zero-cost conclusion. The B2 allergy notice conflicts with the peanut-containing menu, so suspend the affected meals and report to M1, and do not declare safe catering before the substitution is verified and a reply is received.

The handover should state: proposed schedule / proposed purchase, the 20 yuan over authorisation awaiting M1, the 10 damaged portions isolated, the 10 acceptable shortfall awaiting confirmation, and the B2 menu conflict awaiting confirmation. Anomalies must not be closed by re-labelling, deleting the allergy notice, faking replenishment or faking a reply.

The exercise only tests input checking, calculation, staffing plans and anomaly reporting, and does not prove actual food safety, the legality of labour scheduling, occupational qualifications or management competence.

No actual temperature thresholds, allergy diagnoses or safe alternative menus are provided; real food safety and employment conditions must be verified against local regulations, position procedures and the relevant responsible persons. Food acceptance, inventory and hygiene awareness are transferable; cutting and preparation techniques must be learned separately.
Editorial judgement: relatively close, both are food service but the position shifts from management to back-of-house preparation; not a measured transfer distance or qualification exemption.
Need to build restaurant order taking and table service capability
Customer communication, orders and service coordination are transferable; table service / order systems must be practised separately, and tips must be verified locally.
Editorial judgement: relatively close, both are food service but the direction shifts from management to table service; not a measured transfer distance or qualification exemption.
Need to build beverage mixing and alcohol regulation capability
Customer communication, inventory and cleaning are transferable; bartending technique, age verification and local alcohol rules must be learned separately.
Editorial judgement: moderate, requires learning beverage technique and regulatory responsibility; not a measured transfer distance or qualification exemption.

entries.answer: Scope and boundaries | plan, direct or coordinate the activities of an establishment or department that provides food and beverages, managing scheduling, purchasing and acceptance and inventory, service and food preparation quality, budget and payroll, personnel training and complaints. O*NET also lists cooking, clearing tables and food and beverage service when necessary, and some menu design tasks; these overlap with adjacent positions. The occupational classification itself does not confer licensing, professional sign-off or enforcement authority, and specific duties and decision authority must be verified against local regulations and the employer's appointment.
entries.question: What does this occupation actually do?

entries.answer: First-line supervisors of food preparation and serving workers focus on on-site execution supervision for a single shift and specific positions; head chefs and executive chefs are responsible for menus and dish design and kitchen output; lodging managers are responsible for lodging facility operations and guest experience; general and operations managers are responsible for the organisation's overall operations and strategy; food counter attendants (fast food and counter service) and waiters and waitresses and food preparation workers carry out frontline work. This occupation carries the operations, budget, purchasing, menu pricing, personnel and compliance responsibility of the food service department, with authority and outputs different from those occupations.
entries.question: How does it differ from first-line supervisors, head chefs and lodging managers?

entries.answer: Insufficient evidence: no exact Chinese occupational wage and employment values were obtained this round. The US 2025 projection base period is 344,300 people (including 30.6% self-employed), 2035 projected 364,200, growth 5.8%, average annual openings 38,800. May2025 OEWS wage employees 238,430 people with a median annual wage of 69,390 US dollars; the two programmes have different populations. OEWS wages include production bonuses, commissions and tips and exclude overtime, non-production bonuses and employer benefits.

Accommodation and food service urban non-private 62461 and private 55123 yuan / year are industry background only; they cover legal entities with 5 or more persons, are pre-tax and exclude sole proprietors and the self-employed, and cannot substitute for exact occupational or individual wages.

entries.answer: The O*NET work context shows: teamwork extremely important 97%, continuous contact with others 94%, face-to-face discussions every day 93%, working indoors in an environmentally controlled environment every day 91%, dealing with the external public extremely important 84%, making decisions every day 70%, very high responsibility for the work results of others 65%, standing continually 65%, dealing with unpleasant people once a week or more 56%, very high responsibility for the health and safety of other workers 51%, a typical working week of more than 40 hours 41%. Evening and weekend and holiday shifts are common and call-backs are possible; reasonable scheduling and work breaks can manage the burden, but on-site decisions and complaint and employment pressure are real costs.
entries.question: What are the work environment and pressure like?

entries.answer: The impact is mainly in planning and record and reporting steps: scheduling and customer flow forecasting, inventory and purchasing and loss accounting, sales and cost and budget analysis, complaint and work order tracking, and draft training materials and compliance checklists can be assisted by tools; on-site supervision, personnel and employment decisions, complaint and labour dispute handling, and judgements on alcohol and fire safety and licensing compliance remain with managers and responsible persons holding the corresponding duties and authorisation. Task exposure does not equal job replacement.
entries.question: Will AI affect this occupation?

entries.answer: Preparation path suggestion | the US BLS typical preparation is high school or equivalent and relevant experience (less than 5 years in the table) and short-term on-the-job training; the OOH states that food service related experience is usually built first, and some positions accept supplementary education and training. Actual education conditions may differ, and the O*NET answer on education needed is not the education distribution of new hires or a recruitment threshold. The author suggests gradually verifying through team leadership, inventory and cost work and complete simulated records, while promotion and independent decisions depend on employer appointment and local requirements.
entries.question: What education and experience are required?

entries.answer: Jurisdiction check | some US states or localities require food service managers to hold a food safety certification, verified with the local health department. Article 44 of China's Food Safety Law requires food production and operation enterprises to train employees, and Article 45 requires those in contact with directly edible food to undergo an annual examination and obtain a health certificate before taking up the post; the operating licence belongs to the operator, and training or a health certificate does not automatically confer pricing, employment or clinical judgement authority.
entries.question: Are certificates or qualifications required?

entries.answer: Common failures include: non-compliant scheduling and working hours and employment records, uncontrolled purchasing and acceptance and inventory and loss, inadequate management of food preparation and hygiene and temperature and allergens, deficiencies in alcohol and fire safety and licensing compliance, budget and payroll and expenditure over authorisation, and escalating employee conflict and customer complaints. Control points are acting per authorisation and rules with records and pausing, isolating and escalating per procedure; matters involving food safety and licensing and labour disputes are handled by responsible persons holding the corresponding duties and authorisation and by specialist positions and the competent authorities.
entries.question: What are the main risks of this occupation?

entries.answer: US 2025—2035 projected growth is 5.8%, with 38,800 average annual openings including growth and replacement, which is not an individual opportunity guarantee. You can explore first-line supervisor, head chef, lodging or general operations and food service positions; management experience does not automatically bring the target occupation's specialist skills or appointment, and self-employment also requires verification of operating licences, funding and liability.
